title: Farewell Truth and Trust?
author: Michael Albert
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/IMG_0835-680x510.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/05/farewell-
truth-and-trust/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/IMG_0835-680x510.jpeg)

Street art, Portland, Oregon. Photo: Jeffrey St. Clair.

So much going on. Existential crises. Fundamental needs. Short and long term
agendas. Sounds heard all around the world. Much to think about. Much to do.
But does the following also deserve some notice? I think maybe it does.

Truth is under accelerating assault. Trust is dying. Trump lies at every
opportunity. Familiar generalized market duplicity persists. Mainstream media
pervasively manipulates. But something related somehow simultaneously smaller
and larger now grows steadily stronger to also pervert our lives. Something
ridiculously trivial yet also savagely scary threatens to turn us all into
liars or into people who deem lies by others inevitable. Something that makes
us assume fraud is everywhere until we become people who inexorably logically
and defensively distrust and reflexively dismiss all other people. We become
people who hate people.

Here is a personal example. A few weeks ago I had a new book appear on Amazon
and Barnes and Noble. Within a few hours of its appearance, I received a
solicitation about it. The fancy email displayed knowledge of the substance of
my book and of my own history. It offered help. In two days I got ten more
such solicitations. What did it mean?

In my case such solicitations were elaborate emails that admired and praised
the targeted book and author and that offered to help the book reach its
audience for the social good it could do. Eleven such email solicitations in
two days. Each with a signature I didn’t know but by people who were seemingly
from well known institutions.This was new for me. Well, it was almost new.
Such solicitations had actually started to arrive in my email a few weeks
earlier, not for the new book—it was not yet out—but for earlier books.

Some solicitations were pretty ridiculous…one early one was signed by Oprah
Winfrey who wrote me to say she was choosing No Bosses for her book club
selection because of its brilliant and profound message about what to seek
beyond capitalism. An early overshoot. But before long more sophisticated
solicitations with more accurate information about the new book, more
believable writing, and plausible promotion ideas began to arrive.

Amazingly, in subsequent weeks solicitations kept coming and also got steadily
harder to easily brand as the scams they were. They had steadily more
detailed, accurate, and “professionally” presented information about the book
and about me as its author, and their careful, personalized and elaborate
promotional plans got steadily more astute.

At first I would read the emails and consider some of the proposals
plausible—but not being a total dupe, I would also test them. But it got
steadily harder to easily tell or even to discover that they were scams and
before long the effort to test and expose each new solicitation, really any
such solicitation, took so much time and effort that the best policy became to
simply assume every such invitation was a lie that would eventually seek
payment or access. So I went from trusting all emails I got, which had been my
default stance since email first surfaced, to now routinely not trusting
emails.

So what caused this cottage industry of fraudsters to suddenly appear and
grow? AI did. AI is used to incredibly quickly find target books and authors,
to research both, to write letters and in some cases to field replies and
write again and again.

My concern about this trend escalates when I extrapolate from book scams to
all kinds of scams that I can’t even dream of. Selling stuff. Offering stuff.
Needing stuff. I got an email earlier today, still book related, but offering
to translate the new one. Was it real or AI scamming? Then somehow another
approach was tried, and I started to receive letters from radio stations and
station-related clubs offering visibility. No fee required, I just had to
donate. Maybe one or another solicitation/invitation among dozens was real,
but maybe not, and molded to now reflexively distrust, I will never know.

The book scams seek payments to deliver promotional aid that then doesn’t get
done. Phishing scams look for information to access accounts. What’s new is
proliferation and verisimilitude. I received an email two days ago wanting me
to enter information to prevent expiration of an actual subscription I have.
Two more the next day. Scam inflation.

All of this, again, is fueled by AI which the scammer uses to find targets, to
research the target’s needs, to figure out plausible audience for the chosen
books or whatever else the scammer proposes, to write solicitation letters
with elaborate promotional proposals, to answer replies from the scamee, and
so on. Give this cottage industry some more time and it will be making phone
call entreaties. Then FaceTime calls. Whooops. Wait. It already does that.

Estimates now claim there are upwards of 2,500 identified scam operations just
regarding books and their authors. I suspect there are more or else how could
I get so many invites. And that’s just books.

Sometimes the scammer seeks hundreds or maybe a few thousand dollars to be
paid upfront for some service or product. Other times they seek critical
information so as to clean out bank accounts. I got one about an hour ago
saying my Amazon Prime account was being cancelled unless I clicked a provided
link to enter new information. Shortly later I got essentially the same
approach, but for another account. I was urged to go in and fix the
information and of course the email provided a link for the purpose.

The harm that scammers do to their victims is real, very serious, and
accelerating, but it is not the harm I am mainly worrying about in this short
piece. The personal damage every time a scam succeeds is bad enough, but I
have in mind a wider social effect. As scams proliferate so do the domains of
life where it becomes wise to distrust communications. So not only lying but
also distrust spreads.

The former aspect, to fraudulently steal, is rational for the person who wants
to make a buck and sometimes a really big buck—supposing the person has the
moral attributes of a weasel. Such scammers have elaborate web sites. They may
have phone numbers that when the victim calls connect the victim elsewhere
than what the number implies. Such scams are already hard to discern. Imagine
a year or two from now.

The latter aspect, to reflexively distrust, is rational to avoid being ripped
off. We dismiss all requests, offers, and entreaties. If this continues to
proliferate and accelerate the social effects will grow as well. We aren’t
what we eat but we do tend to become what we do. And so we slip slide into a
world in which truth and trust are each assassinated. But who benefits if we
each believe everyone else is a liar? You may think no one does, but no, the
best liars benefit, and also all elites benefit because solidarity requires
trust which takes a killing blow.

So I think that alongside war, repression, escalating misogyny, racism, and
political obfuscation and manipulation, as if all that wasn’t enough, we now
have a slowly but steadily growing epidemic of deception that causes good,
caring people to assume that everyone else is an exploitative deceiver.

At exactly the moment when we need to grow solidarity we instead turn inward.
It turns out that there may be a method to lots of what looks like madness.
The state prosecutes immigrants, the poor, and dissenters with great vigor. It
searches, labels, and rounds up “its enemies.” Meanwhile fraud-fueled
corruption runs free. The state ignores our enemies or even abets them.
Regarding scams, don’t punish the perps, but instead protect them all the way
from Trump down. Make mistrust “sensible” at every level.

I hate to write anything pointing out ills without suggesting possible paths
to win better, but I have to admit I am unsure how to positively react to the
observations offered above. To tell people to be smart, to not get fooled,
okay—but when that takes the form of don’t believe anyone who seems nice,
anyone who seems supportive, anyone who offers you something positive, because
fraud is everywhere—then the advice seems likely to aggravate our social
trajectory of distrust and atomization. It seems to build in us an inclination
to suspect and dismiss at precisely the moment when we most need caring
solidarity.

So I am unsure what to suggest. How can we warn people about the growing
“quality” of scammers and yet urge people to collectively care about one
another and work together? It is clear how a movement can constructively
oppose proliferating AI data centers. How does a movement constructively
address proliferating AI truth and trust assassins? Soon, of course, some
scammers will offer to protect us against other scammers.

Maybe how to deal with truth and trust decay needs a little thought along with
what tactics, what organizational choices, and what strategies we should use
to stop Trump, stop fascism, stop ecological collapse, stop impoverishment,
stop misogyny, stop racism and then to replace the oppressive institutions
that give rise to all that?

And P.S. it really is all one fight. Fascism thrives on lies and mistrust.
Indeed, fascism can’t live without them. And our American brand of Trumpian
Fascism seems to not even believe or have its adherents believe that there is
any actual truth at all. How else can we explain that Trump says the things he
does despite that so much of what he says is so transparently false?

The Covid vaccine didn’t work. Vaccines cause autism, but hydroxychloroquine
worked, and so did ivermectin.

Prescription drug prices are down by 2,000 percent.

Foreign countries pay our tariffs.

Fauci killed millions of people.

Climate change is a hoax.

Wind power caused a massive TV blackout during the Trump-Biden debate.

Solar power is useless because the sun doesn’t shine at night, and batteries
don’t exist.

I invaded Los Angeles and now California’s water is flowing.

Portland is on fire, it needs my help.

Every drug boat in the Caribbean ‘kills 25,000 Americans’

Obama, Biden and Comey made up the Epstein files.

Smoke blanketed North America because Canada didn’t rake its 2 million square
miles of forest.

Climate change is a Chinese hoax.

We’ve destroyed Iran’s military, and the Iranian regime is begging for a deal.

The economy is in a “golden age.” Prices are down.

I, Trump have a 59 percent approval rating.

I won the 2020 election.

The US is ‘the only country in the world’ with mail-in voting.

I, Trump am a stable genius.

And lately, “my dad was born in Germany” which would be fine except that
Trump’s dad was actually born in New York City.

And so on.

Truth becomes whatever Trump or whoever proclaims it to be. Does Trump believe
his dad was born in Germany when he says so, and that he was born in NYC when
he says that? Truth is apparently whatever the biggest boss says it is.

Duck and cover. Alone. Dismiss everyone. Or what?
